unresolved.finding: The file contains one author record but has no terminating newline (wc -l reports 0), which can cause awkward concatenation in line-oriented tooling.
The changelog delegates the complete history to `svn log` without identifying a repository URL, revision, or snapshot date, so this asset is not independently usable for release provenance.
Both stages pin to the EOL CentOS 7 image, leaving the build/runtime base dependent on an unsupported distribution.
`yum update` and unversioned package installs are used without repository snapshots or package pins, so identical image builds can change over time.
The image installs OpenMPI development/runtime packages but configures XBeach with `--without-mpi`; the intentional reason and supported parallel-mode contract are not stated.
The image clones the mutable GitHub `mmi` branch and installs it without a commit or release pin.
The container installs the `mmi` Python package and invokes `mmi-runner` with a hard-coded port range, but does not document required input layout or how the exposed ports are used.

This is an uncustomized GNU INSTALL template: it points readers to a package README for XBeach-specific prerequisites/options, but provides no XBeach compiler, NetCDF, MPI, precision, or supported-platform contract.
The document presents `make check`, `make installcheck`, `make uninstall`, and `make distcheck` as possible workflows without stating which targets this snapshot actually implements.
The boilerplate copyright range ends at 2013 and is not tied to a package release or generator version, leaving provenance of this copied installation document unclear.
The file is the unmodified LGPL-2.1 text but does not identify XBeach, the covered components, copyright holders, or whether the license applies to the complete repository versus selected libraries.
The file ends with generic instructions and placeholder notices for a new library, rather than a project-specific notice or pointer to the actual source-level licensing terms.
The file provides no release-specific news and redirects to an unversioned HTTP website, so readers cannot recover snapshot-era release information reliably.
The bootstrap wrapper has no explicit shell strictness, tool/version check, or diagnostic guidance, leaving failures and required Autotools versions implicit.
The generated page omits a doctype, charset, title, and viewport metadata, leaving standards mode and basic accessibility/metadata behavior unclear.
The selector begins immediately after the closing rule as `} html>body`, an old browser-specific CSS hack that is syntactically unusual and not explained.
`${list}` is inserted raw inside HTML with no documented escaping contract, so correctness depends on the generator guaranteeing HTML-safe list content.
The introductory description contains multiple typos and an incomplete phrase (`is spacepars`, `mnemonic is know`, `distribute`), making the generated-variable contract harder to interpret.

The generator workflow describes templates and generated files but does not state whether checked-in generated files must be regenerated, how stale outputs are detected, or which Makefile target enforces consistency.
The non-make example hard-codes an `f90` compiler command without specifying required Fortran standard/features or the compiler options needed by this generator.
The primary documentation is delegated to an unpinned external ReadTheDocs URL, with no version or commit identifying which manual matches this source snapshot.
The Git example uses `git commit -a .` and `git push .`, which do not identify a normal commit message or remote and are likely unusable as written.
The SVN workflow is presented against a GitHub repository without clarifying the supported GitHub SVN endpoint or authentication/push limitations.
The file stops at a statement that the DOC/PDF manual is deprecated and gives no replacement-version mapping or offline documentation path.
The MPI build instructions name `--with-mpi` but do not state the MPI implementation/compiler wrapper, NetCDF/MPI prerequisites, or how this option changes the generated build.
The instruction to run only `make clean` between MPI configurations may leave configure-generated state and dependency files from the previous configuration.
The dependency generator is explicitly described as not bullet-proof, but no known failure modes or required manual dependency checks are provided.
`USEMPI` is described as a macro without specifying its exact compiler-definition syntax or whether it is generated exclusively by configure.

The document says `sglobal` is unfilled on non-master processes while also saying distribution descriptors are available in both `sglobal` and `slocal`; the valid fields and access rules are not clearly distinguished.

The proposed replacement for saved scratch arrays omits a deallocation example and assumes automatic removal at subroutine exit, while the original saved allocation can retain dimensions across calls; callers with changing local-grid sizes therefore lack a safe lifecycle contract.

The claim that post-allocation initialization such as `xyz = 0` is superfluous is unsafe: allocatable numeric arrays are not generally initialized by allocation, so removing it can expose undefined values.

The Windows MPI guidance is tied to MPICH2, Visual Fortran project tabs, fixed `C:\Program Files\MPICH2\` paths, and legacy symbol/decorated-library names without identifying the supported toolchain or snapshot.
The document says unresolved code locations are marked `wwvv`, but does not enumerate them or provide a cross-reference, making the warning markers difficult to audit.
The promised comprehensive parallelization report is stated as future work with no date or linked artifact.

The document asserts that XBeach uses double precision everywhere while describing the nonstandard `real*8` representation, but does not identify the compiler flags/kind policy that enforce this across the codebase.
The guidance focuses on literal promotion but does not address modern kind-parameter practice or compiler-dependent literal evaluation, leaving the stated precision policy incomplete for portability.
The claim that an integer exponent is more efficient and that a real exponent may force `exp`/`log` is compiler/code-generation dependent and is presented without qualification or benchmark context.
The explanatory parenthetical beginning at line 126 is not closed, making the final example structurally unclear.
The entry instruction contains a typo (`teh`) and gives no indication of the expected working directory or failure handling for `./bootstrap`.

The required-file list names `COPYING`, `README`, and several build files/directories, while this shard provides `LICENSE` instead of `COPYING`; the document does not distinguish repository-wide prerequisites from files expected in this snapshot.

This is a 2000 netCDF version-3 man page containing legacy CRAY/UNICOS and Majordomo instructions, with no indication of the bundled library version or whether the documented interface matches the linked NetCDF-Fortran installation.
The `nf90_create` synopsis omits the optional `initialsize` and `chunksize` arguments that are described immediately below, leaving the callable interface inconsistent within the same entry.
The `nf90_rename_var` prototype contains malformed roff/text (`intent9in)` and parameter `name` versus `newname`), so generated documentation cannot be trusted for this routine's signature.
The `nf90_put_var` and `nf90_get_var` prototypes use the literal placeholder `<<whatever>>` for the polymorphic data argument, providing no compilable or type-resolution-level interface.
The `nf90_put_att` prototype likewise uses `<<whatever>>`, while the prose lists supported kinds without documenting how the generic Fortran interface dispatches them.
The `nf90_get_att` declaration contains malformed roff (`\` followed by `fIvalues`) and does not render a valid argument markup.
The `nf90_rename_att` entry has an unterminated `(Corresponds to ...)` roff construct and lacks a visible closing `.RE` before the next `.HP` entry, so formatting and section boundaries are broken.

Although status-returning functions are introduced, the routine descriptions do not consistently state which invalid states/arguments produce errors or whether output arguments are defined after a nonzero status.
The filter suppresses matching warning lines but unconditionally exits 0, so upstream tooling cannot distinguish a successful filter from an input/read/grep failure.
The expression removes any line matching `warning:.*mpi_` without documenting case sensitivity, compiler format assumptions, or whether warning counts are expected to remain visible elsewhere.

The cleanup script recursively targets `Makefile.in` and unconditionally removes all files under `config/*` plus selected build files, but does not verify the working tree or protect hand-maintained files.

The script operates relative to the caller's current directory rather than its own repository location and has no strict mode or confirmation, so invoking it from the wrong directory can affect unrelated files.
The `find ... | xargs rm -f` pipeline depends on POSIX/GNU command behavior and does not handle unusual filenames safely.

A `compatibility` element is nested inside `dependentAssembly`, where the manifest structure normally expects dependency metadata; whether this empty nested declaration is accepted by the Windows loader is not established here.
The manifest hard-codes an amd64 identity and a fixed set of Windows supported-OS GUIDs without documenting the generator build target or behavior on 32-bit/other Windows versions.
The directory-preservation note has no terminating newline (wc -l reports 0), which can cause awkward concatenation in line-oriented tooling.
The baseline version record is explicitly `Range 000`, date `0000/00/00 00:00:00`, and URL `UNKNOWN`, so binaries built from it cannot carry meaningful source provenance.

The version template relies on `$WCRANGE$`, `$WCDATE$`, `$WCURL$`, and conditional keyword substitutions without documenting the generator/version-control system or behavior when any placeholder remains unresolved.

The three build metadata fields are fixed at length 1024 with no stated truncation/validation policy, so unusually long revision, date, or URL values may be silently clipped or mishandled by consumers.
